newsitem.title: USA: HEALTH - Wine may reduce breast cancer risk.
newsitem.headline: HEALTH - Wine may reduce breast cancer risk.

text.p: A wine industry group suggested on Monday that a compound found in wine may reduce the risk of breast cancer, but an article in a medical journal said alcohol increased the risk.

Speaking at a luncheon presentation sponsored by the San Francisco-based Wine Institute, researcher Roy Williams released new experimental findings showing that trans-resveratrol, a compound found in both red and white wine, may have a role in preventing breast cancer.

This compound "has anti-estrogenic properties which may offer a measure of protection against hormone-dependent cancers such as breast cancer," Williams said in a statement. He is based at Old Dominion University in Norfolk, Virginia.
Williams has conducted several laboratory tests using trans-resveratrol on two types of cultured human breast cancer cells.

Epidemiologist Curtis Ellison of Boston University, also speaking at the Wine Institute event, cited several studies over the last decade that found that moderate wine-drinking may reduce the risk of breast cancer, while consumption of hard liquor or beer increased the risk.

But Bonnie Liebman of the Centre for Science in the Public Interest said results from test tube studies and animals were no substitute for studies on humans and "the evidence in people points in the exact opposite direction."
"Even moderate amounts of alcohol seem to increase the risk of breast cancer," Liebman said by telephone.

An article in this month's issue of the journal Epidemiology, provided by the institute, said, "Our data add support to the accumulating evidence that alcohol consumption is associated with increased risk of breast cancer and further indicate that alcohol acts at a late stage in breast carcinogenesis."
